{"id": "9b7f75ad-c4f3-46f3-b3fa-24d26ea25fb1", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_7uuDVaP5CykpEhCN2mk5lY", "content": "[{'text': '## Documentation search results\\n\\n{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Monitor network performance for ENA settings on your EC2 instance\",\"context\":\"# Monitor network performance for ENA settings on your EC2 instance\\\\n\\\\nThe Elastic Network Adapter (ENA) driver publishes network performance metrics from the\\\\ninstances where they are enabled. You can use these metrics to troubleshoot instance\\\\nperformance issues, choose the right instance size for a workload, plan scaling activities\\\\nproactively, and benchmark applications to determine whether they maximize the performance\\\\navailable on an instance.\\\\n\\\\nAmazon EC2 defines network maximums at the instance level to ensure a high-quality networking\\\\nexperience, including consistent network performance across instance sizes. AWS provides\\\\nmaximums for the following for each instance:\\\\n\\\\n* Bandwidth capability \u2013 Each EC2 instance has\\\\n a maximum bandwidth for aggregate inbound and outbound traffic, based on instance\\\\n type and size. Some instances use a network I/O credit mechanism to allocate network\\\\n bandwidth based on average bandwidth utilization. Amazon EC2 also has maximum bandwidth\\\\n for traffic to Direct Connect and the internet. For more information, see Amazon EC2 instance network bandwidth.\\\\n* Packet-per-second (PPS) performance \u2013 Each\\\\n EC2 instance has a maximum PPS performance, based on instance type and size.\\\\n* Connections tracked \u2013 The security group\\\\n tracks each connection established to ensure that return packets are delivered as\\\\n expected. There is a maximum number of connections that can be tracked per instance.\\\\n For more information, see Amazon EC2 security group connection tracking\\\\n* Link-local service access \u2013 Amazon EC2 provides a\\\\n maximum PPS per network interface for traffic to local proxy services such as the\\\\n Amazon DNS service, the Instance Metadata Service, and the Amazon Time Sync Service.\\\\n\\\\nWhen the network traffic for an instance exceeds a maximum, AWS shapes the traffic that\\\\nexceeds the maximum by queueing and then dropping network packets. You can monitor when traffic exceeds a maximum using the network\\\\nperformance metrics. These metrics inform you, in real time, of impact to network traffic\\\\nand possible network performance issues.\\\\n\\\\n###### Contents\\\\n\\\\n* Requirements\\\\n* Metrics for the ENA driver\\\\n* View the network performance metrics for your instance\\\\n* Metrics for ENA Express\\\\n* Network performance metrics with the DPDK driver for ENA\\\\n* Metrics on instances running FreeBSD\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/monitoring-network-performance-ena.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Amazon EC2 instance-level network performance metrics uncover new insights | Networking & Content Delivery\",\"context\":\"## Network Performance Metrics\\\\n\\\\nAdditional instance level network performance metrics are available on instances using ENA both for Windows and Linux operating systems. These include:\\\\n\\\\n* ***bw_in_allowance_exceeded*** and ***bw_out_allowance_exceeded*** indicates the number of packets that are queued or dropped because of instance aggregate bandwidth exceeded BW allowance for the instance.\\\\n* ***pps_allowance_exceeded*** indicates number of packets queued or dropped due to Packet Per Second (PPS) exceeding the allowance for the instance. PPS allowance is enforced separately to the overall bandwidth allowance and, while the instance may still be under overall bandwidth allowance, the PPS allowance may exceed if the mean packet size is small.\\\\n* ***conntrack_allowance_exceeded*** indicates the number of packets dropped due to exhaustion of tracked session allowance for the instance, new sessions will fail to establish once this allowance is exceeded. Sessions are restored once instance session count drops below the allowance.\\\\n* ***linklocal_allowance_exceeded*** indicates the number of packets dropped due to PPS rate allowance exceeded for local services such as Route 53 DNS Resolver, Instance Metadata Service, Amazon Time Sync Service. This often points to suboptimal design choices or misconfiguration. This allowance is the same across instances.\\\\n\\\\nIf any of the above counters, except for ***linklocal_allowance_exceeded***, are incrementing at a noticeable rate, it\u2019s advisable to go up an instance family (for example, a c5n.18xlarge instead of c5n.9xlarge). All of these allowances get a bump as you increase instance size within the instance family, except for link local PPS. If the instance is behind a load balancer, horizontal scaling to add additional instances and distribute the network load is another strategy to consider. In this case, you might also use a Gateway Load Balancer to automatically scale instances of appliances that are used for inline inspection of network traffic.\\\\n\\\\nNew metrics support is part of ENA driver version 2.2.10 or later for Linux and 2.2.2.0 or later for Windows (2.2.2.0 will be available soon). Recent Amazon Linux 2 AMIs come with latest ENA drivers by default, eliminating the need to manually update the ENA driver. CloudWatch Agent version 1.246396.0 and later natively support export of these metrics directly from the instance. This can be used for visualization in CloudWatch dashboards, or to\\\\n\\\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/networking-and-content-delivery/amazon-ec2-instance-level-network-performance-metrics-uncover-new-insights/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Nitro system considerations for performance tuning\",\"context\":\"#### Application design considerations\\\\n\\\\nThere are aspects of application design and configuration that can affect your\\\\nprocessing efficiency. The following list includes some important\\\\nconsiderations.\\\\n\\\\n**Packet size**\\\\n: Larger packet sizes can increase throughput for the data that an\\\\n instance can send and receive on the network. Amazon EC2 supports jumbo\\\\n frames of 9001 bytes, however other services may enforce different\\\\n limits. Smaller packet sizes can increase the packet process rate,\\\\n but this can reduce the maximum achieved bandwidth when the number\\\\n of packets exceed PPS allowances.\\\\n\\\\n If the size of a packet exceeds the Maximum Transmission Unit\\\\n (MTU) of a network hop, a router along the path might fragment it.\\\\n The resulting packet fragments are considered exceptions, and are\\\\n normally processed at the standard rate (not accelerated). This can\\\\n cause variations in your performance. However, you can override the\\\\n standard behavior for outbound fragmented packets with the fragment\\\\n proxy mode setting. For more information, see Maximize network performance on your Nitro system. We recommended that\\\\n you evaluate your topology when you configure MTU.\\\\n\\\\n**Protocol trade-offs**\\\\n: Reliable protocols like TCP have more overhead than unreliable\\\\n protocols like UDP. The lower overhead and simplified network\\\\n processing for the UDP transport protocol can result in a higher PPS\\\\n rate, but at the expense of reliable packet delivery. If reliable\\\\n packet delivery isn\u2019t critical for your application, UDP might be a\\\\n good option.\\\\n\\\\n**Micro-bursting**\\\\n: Micro-bursting occurs when traffic exceeds allowances during brief\\\\n periods of time rather than being evenly distributed. This typically\\\\n happens on a microsecond scale.\\\\n\\\\n For example, say that you have an instance that can send up to 10\\\\n Gbps, and your application sends the full 10 Gb in half a second.\\\\n This micro-burst exceeds the allowance during the first half second\\\\n and leaves nothing for the remainder of the second. Even though you\\\\n sent 10Gb in the 1 second timeframe, allowances in the first half\\\\n second can result in packets being queued or dropped.\\\\n\\\\n You can use a network scheduler such as Linux Traffic Control to\\\\n help pace your throughput and avoid causing queued or dropped\\\\n packets as a result of micro-bursting.\\\\n\\\\n**Number of flows**\\\\n: A single flow is limited to 5\\\\n\\\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ena-nitro-perf.html\"}]}}\\n\\n## Recent AWS announcements (What\\'s New)\\n\\nNewer than your training data may be. When these conflict with the documentation results above or with what you remember, prefer the most recent dated source.\\n\\n{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"ENA Express for AWS GovCloud (US) Regions - AWS\",\"context\":\"AWS has introduced ENA Express, a new network interface for EC2 instances in AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, which utilizes the SRD (scalable reliable datagram) protocol to enhance network performance. ENA Express offers higher single flow bandwidth and lower tail latency for network traffic between EC2 instances, particularly beneficial for workloads like databases, file systems, and distributed storage systems. Previously, customers could use multipath TCP to increase bandwidth, but it adds complexity and may not be compatible with application layers. SRD, a proprietary protocol, delivers these improvements through congestion control, multi-pathing, and packet reordering directly from the Nitro card. Enabling ENA Express is a straightforward configuration, requiring a single command or console toggle for EC2 instances. The SRD protocol increases the maximum single flow bandwidth and improves tail latencies for high throughput workloads, working transparently with TCP and UDP protocols. ENA Express is available in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions at no additional cost. ENA Express utilizes the AWS Scalable Reliable Datagram (SRD) protocol for improved network performance, which is also used by Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) io2 Block Express and Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) for high performance computing and machine learning workloads. ENA Express is available for all supported instance types and sizes in various regions including Africa, Asia Pacific, Canada, Europe, Israel, Mexico, US East, US West, and AWS GovCloud. This feature comes at no additional cost and is designed for workloads such as distributed storage, databases, and file systems that require deployments spanning multiple Availability Zones for resilience. ENA Express establishes an SRD connection when both communicating instances have ENA Express enabled and uses multi-pathing to route traffic across the network, avoiding head-of-line blocking. {"id": "068134b5-a15a-44fe-81a3-7694ddc22293", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "No, this isn't necessarily a misconfiguration — 20,000-byte segments in a tcpdump capture are expected even with a correctly set 9001-byte MTU, and here's why:

**It's TCP Segmentation Offload (TSO), not a misconfigured MTU**

- `tcpdump` on Linux captures packets **before** they're handed to the NIC driver for final segmentation when Generalized/TCP Segmentation Offload (GSO/TSO) is enabled. The kernel builds a large "superpacket" (often up to 64KB) and hands it off to the network stack as one unit; the actual splitting into MTU-sized frames happens later, in the NIC hardware or driver (on EC2, the ENA driver).
- So what you're capturing is the pre-segmentation buffer, not what actually goes out on the wire. The real frames transmitted are still ≤9001 bytes — AWS confirms EC2 supports jumbo frames up to 9001 bytes, and anything above the path's MTU would normally be fragmented or dropped (not silently sent oversized).
- This is standard behavior on Linux hosts with ENA (and virtually all modern NICs) and isn't specific to a bug or bad config.

**How to confirm it's TSO/GSO and not an actual oversized-frame problem:**
1. Check offload settings: `ethtool -k eth0 | grep -E "tcp-segmentation|generic-segmentation|large-receive"`
2. If you want tcpdump to show real on-wire frame sizes, either disable offloads temporarily (`ethtool -K eth0 tso off gso off gro off`) and re-capture, or capture with `-s 0` and inspect at a point downstream (e.g., on a different host, or via a mirrored port) where offload has already been applied.
3. Verify actual path MTU with `tracepath` or `ping -M do -s 8973 <dest>` (9001 - 28 bytes overhead) to confirm no fragmentation/drops are happening in practice.

So: the 9001 MTU is very likely fine. The 20,000-byte segments are a capture artifact of TSO/GSO offload, not evidence of misconfiguration.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
